title: Smart tab sleeping
one_line_goal: Four tab-sleeping strategies built safely and compared on the test bench
summary: Ferrum learns to put unused tabs to sleep, and later close them while remembering their place, without ever losing your work. Four strategies (never, fixed timer, memory pressure, cost-aware) run in one app and are compared on the test bench. Similar ideas already exist, so we also finish the literature check.

tasks.title: Tab state machine
tasks.what: The rules for each tab's state: active, background, idle, close candidate, closed, restoring, and which moves between them are allowed.
tasks.why: Each tab must always be in one clear state, and the tab you are using must never be closed by mistake.
tasks.how: Write the allowed moves as a fixed table in plain Rust code, with tests for every allowed and forbidden move and for random event sequences.
tasks.chain: Each tab must always be in one clear state (active, background, idle, close candidate, closed, restoring) → write the allowed moves as a fixed table with tests → the tab you are using can never be closed by mistake.
tasks.check: Tests cover every allowed and forbidden move, plus random sequences that never break the rules.

tasks.title: Signals for sleep decisions
tasks.what: Inputs for sleep decisions: last use, memory pressure, tab activity, cost to restore, media playing, downloads, your exclusions and unsaved forms.
tasks.why: Each strategy needs real signals with known limits to decide well.
tasks.how: Build one provider per signal, tested on fake inputs and test pages; per-tab cost can only be estimated, and some Windows and WebView2 signals are not yet confirmed.
tasks.chain: Good decisions need inputs → measure last use, memory pressure, tab activity, cost to restore, media playing, downloads, your exclusions and unsaved forms → each strategy decides on real signals with known limits.
tasks.check: Each signal has tests with fake inputs and with a test page; its limits are written down.

tasks.title: Sleep actions: hide, suspend, close, restore
tasks.what: The sleep actions: hide, suspend, low-memory mode, close while remembering address, history and scroll position, and restore.
tasks.why: Sleeping has levels, so each strategy can pick the right one for a tab.
tasks.how: Use WebView2's suspend and low-memory settings (never both together), close the web view to discard, and test each action and that restore returns to the same page.
tasks.chain: Sleeping has levels → build hide, suspend, low-memory mode and close-but-remember (address, history, scroll position), plus restore → each strategy can pick the right level.
tasks.check: Tests confirm the web view's state after each action and that restore returns to the same page.

tasks.title: Safety guards
tasks.what: Guards that stop a tab from being closed while media plays, a download runs, a form is unsaved, the page asks before leaving, or you excluded the site.
tasks.why: Closing a tab in the middle of a task can lose your work; sleeping must never cost you data.
tasks.how: Check each guard before any close, test that guarded pages are never closed under any strategy or memory pressure, and log each refusal with its reason.
tasks.chain: Closing a tab mid-task can lose your work → never close a tab while media plays, a download runs, a form is unsaved, the page asks before leaving, or you excluded the site → sleeping never costs you data.
tasks.check: Guarded test pages are never closed under any strategy, even under memory pressure; each refusal is logged.

tasks.title: Three simple strategies
tasks.what: Three simple strategies: never sleep, sleep after a fixed idle time, and sleep under memory pressure, chosen by a setting.
tasks.why: They are the baselines the smarter strategy is compared against, and one app runs them all so only the strategy differs.
tasks.how: Build each strategy behind a run-time setting in the same app, and test each on scripted signal timelines.
tasks.chain: We need baselines to compare against → build never sleep, sleep after a fixed idle time, and sleep under memory pressure, switchable by a setting → one app runs every strategy, so only the strategy differs.
tasks.check: Tests per strategy on scripted timelines pass; one build switches strategy by setting.

tasks.title: Cost-aware strategy
tasks.what: A smarter, cost-aware strategy that weighs memory saved, energy and restore delay in one weighted score.
tasks.why: Fixing the weights on separate calibration workloads means the strategy is not tuned to the test it is judged on.
tasks.how: Compute the score from documented measurements, set the energy weight to zero if energy cannot be measured, and commit the weights before the campaign.
tasks.chain: Smarter choices weigh memory saved, energy and restore delay → combine them in one weighted score (energy weight zero if energy cannot be measured) and fix the weights on separate calibration workloads → the strategy is not tuned to the test it is judged on.
tasks.check: Score tests pass; weights and calibration method saved before the campaign; calibration and test workloads do not overlap.

tasks.title: Log every sleep decision
tasks.what: A log of every tab state change and every refusal, plus the time from starting a restore to the restored page showing its first content.
tasks.why: We must see what each strategy did, and how long restores take, to compare them.
tasks.how: Record each change in the record format from the telemetry phase, and test it on a scripted close and restore.
tasks.chain: We must see what each strategy did → record every state change and refusal, and the time from restore to first content → behaviour and restore delay become measurable.
tasks.check: A scripted close and restore produce the expected records and a restore-time record.

tasks.title: Long-running test
tasks.what: A long-running test with many background tabs under each strategy, watching memory growth, crashes and restore success.
tasks.why: Some problems only show up after hours of use.
tasks.how: Run the many-background-tabs workload for a long session per strategy, save the raw output, and turn each crash or failed restore into a fixed bug with a test before the campaign.
tasks.chain: Some problems only show up over hours → run many background tabs for a long session under each strategy, watching memory growth, crashes and restores → every bug found is fixed, with a test, before the campaign.
tasks.check: Raw output saved; every crash or failed restore has a fix and a test.

tasks.title: Bench settings for each strategy
tasks.what: Test-bench settings for each Ferrum strategy: fixed idle time, memory pressure and cost-aware.
tasks.why: The only difference between Ferrum runs must be the strategy switch.
tasks.how: Add one settings file per strategy, check their format, and confirm with a diff report that only the strategy setting differs.
tasks.chain: The test bench needs a setup per strategy → add one settings file for each Ferrum strategy → the only difference between Ferrum runs is the strategy switch.
tasks.check: Settings files pass the format check; the diff shows only the strategy switch differs.

tasks.title: Write predictions before testing
tasks.what: Predictions for the strategy comparison written down in advance, with the size of difference that would really matter.
tasks.why: Deciding what counts as success after seeing the data is biased; writing it first means results cannot be bent to fit.
tasks.how: Mark every linked prediction as preregistered (written in advance) and get your approval before the campaign starts.
tasks.chain: Deciding what counts as success after seeing data is biased → write each prediction and its meaningful-difference threshold first, and you approve them → results cannot be bent to fit.
tasks.check: Every prediction is recorded and approved by you before the campaign starts.

tasks.title: Strategy campaign
tasks.what: The strategy campaign: the four strategies run on identical workloads, with Chrome and Edge as shipped for reference.
tasks.why: It produces the raw data on tab sleeping that the paper analyses.
tasks.how: Run it with the test runner under the same rules as the first campaign, saving the run record, every trial and checksums; nothing is interpreted yet.
tasks.chain: Bench and predictions are ready → run the four strategies on identical workloads, with Chrome and Edge as shipped for reference → raw data for P8.
tasks.check: A complete raw-data folder with every trial and checksums; no results stated yet.

tasks.title: Literature check: what is really new
tasks.what: A closing literature check comparing our approach with similar ideas: Chrome and Edge tab sleeping, Android app standby, cost-aware caching and earlier reading.
tasks.why: The paper may claim only what is truly new, and similar ideas already exist.
tasks.how: List each close earlier idea with a verified source, say what (if anything) differs, and get your approval of the assessment.
tasks.chain: Similar ideas exist (Chrome and Edge tab sleeping, Android app standby, cost-aware caching) → compare our approach with each, using verified sources, and you approve the assessment → the paper claims only what is truly new.
tasks.check: Every close earlier work is listed with a verified source and what differs; your approval recorded.

tasks.title: Optional rerun with smart sleeping
tasks.what: An optional rerun of the footprint, page-load, smoothness, energy and reliability experiments with smart sleeping switched on.
tasks.why: The first campaign tested Ferrum without sleeping; this rerun fills that gap, or the gap is recorded as a known limitation.
tasks.how: Only if you pick option (a) in [this open question](ref:Q-208): same rules as the first campaign, new shuffled blocks never mixed with the first data, sealed when done.
tasks.chain: The first campaign tested Ferrum without sleeping → if you pick option (a) in [this open question](ref:Q-208), rerun footprint, page-load, smoothness, energy and reliability with smart sleeping, same rules, kept separate → otherwise the gap is recorded as a known limitation.
tasks.check: A sealed raw-data folder with every trial, or a written deviation note that cites your answer.

tasks.title: Gate and your review
tasks.what: The end-of-phase check and your review of the tab-sleeping work.
tasks.why: The paper phase starts only after every check passes and you have approved this phase.
tasks.how: The gate script runs every check and saves the evidence; you review it and approve the end of this phase.
tasks.chain: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review and approve; only then does P8 start.
tasks.check: All evidence files exist, the wiki check is clean, and you approve the end of P7.

test_gate.explanation: Code and tests pass → safety guards hold under every strategy → sleep actions behave as tested → earlier features still work → you work with smart sleeping on and report any lost state → you approve weights, predictions and the novelty check → you approve. Only then does P8 start.

rows.proves: Code is tidy and warning-free, all automatic tests pass, and the release build works.
Third-party libraries have acceptable licences and no known security problems.
No guarded tab is ever closed, in tests or in the long run.
Each action leaves the web view in the expected state.
Security, measurement accuracy, tabs and browsing tests still pass.
The analysis code still passes its tests.
The plan pages are consistent and have no broken links.
You work with smart sleeping on and report any lost state or surprising close.
You approved the weights, the predictions and the novelty check.
